label: Active Directory
summary: A Windows domain over LDAP, read-only: domain controllers and FSMO roles, privileged group members, password policy, and security findings such as Kerberos-roastable accounts, unconstrained delegation or an old krbtgt password.

credentials.label: Service account
credentials.help: A plain domain user created for DumbMonit, member of no group.

fields.help: The user principal name (svc-dumbmonit@corp.example.com), DOMAIN\svc-dumbmonit, or the full DN.

fields.label: Password
fields.help: Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Create a read-only service account for DumbMonit
steps:
Active Directory Users and Computers → your domain → Users → New → User: name it as follows, set a long random password and add it to no group.
svc-dumbmonit
On its Account tab, tick Password never expires, or the bind fails the day the password does.

Optional, to see inbound replication status: grant the account the right listed below on the domain object.
dsacls "DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" /G "CORP\svc-dumbmonit:CA;Monitor active directory replication"
For LDAPS, export your certification authority's certificate as Base-64 encoded X.509 and paste it as CA certificate below.
In DumbMonit, enter a domain controller's name as its certificate names it (dc1.corp.example.com) and log in as svc-dumbmonit@corp.example.com.

ports.purpose: LDAPS (default), also to the other domain controllers
Only with the StartTLS or plain LDAP option
Only with the DNS servers option
Only with the DNS servers option

permissions:
Domain Users membership only
No group or delegation is needed to read

Monitor active directory replication
Optional: inbound replication status
setup.warning: Plain LDAP on port 389 sends the password in clear and is refused by default: use LDAPS, or StartTLS on port 389.

options.label: Connection security
options.help: ldaps (port 636) encrypts from the first byte; starttls upgrades port 389 before logging in; plain sends the password in clear text and needs Allow plain LDAP.

options.label: Port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port: 636 for LDAPS, 389 otherwise.

options.label: CA certificate
options.help: The PEM certificate (Base-64 encoded X.509) of the authority that issued the domain controllers' certificates. Only that authority is then trusted.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Skips every certificate check: the connection stays encrypted, but anyone on the path could pose as the domain controller. Prefer the CA certificate above.

options.label: Allow plain LDAP
options.help: Required for the plain setting: the service account's password then crosses the network readable by anyone on the path.

options.label: DNS servers
options.help: Optional. IP addresses of the DNS servers that know the domain (comma-separated). Every name lookup of this monitor then goes through them instead of the system resolver; empty keeps the system DNS.

options.label: Check every domain controller
options.help: Opens a connection to the LDAP port of each domain controller of the domain, to alert when one stops answering. Names that do not resolve from DumbMonit are reported, not alerted on.

options.label: Inactive user after (days)
options.help: An enabled user with no logon for this long is counted as inactive. The last-logon date can lag by up to 14 days.

options.label: Inactive computer after (days)
options.help: An enabled computer with no logon for this long is counted as inactive.

options.label: Full inventory every (minutes)
options.help: Every user and computer is read in the background at this pace (1 to 1440); health is read at every check.

options.label: Timeout (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each LDAP operation, from 1 to 60.

setup.title: Enable Apache's mod_status
steps:
Enable mod_status (it ships with Apache and is usually on already).
a2enmod status

Add this location to the Apache configuration, restricted to the DumbMonit host (adjust the address).
<Location "/server-status">
SetHandler server-status
Require ip 10.0.0.5
</Location>

Optional: turn on the request and byte counters.
ExtendedStatus On

Reload Apache, then open http://apache.lan/server-status?auto from the DumbMonit host.
apachectl graceful
In DumbMonit, enter the Apache host, for example apache.lan, and the path if it is not /server-status.

setup.title: Let DumbMonit read CrowdSec's metrics
steps:
Make the metrics reachable: set listen_addr in the prometheus section of /etc/crowdsec/config.yaml to an address DumbMonit can reach, then restart CrowdSec.
sudo sed -i 's/listen_addr: 127.0.0.1/listen_addr: 0.0.0.0/' /etc/crowdsec/config.yaml
sudo systemctl restart crowdsec

Check from the DumbMonit host that the metrics answer on port 6060, and filter that port so only the DumbMonit host reaches it.
curl -s http://crowdsec.lan:6060/metrics | grep cs_info
DumbMonit also checks the Local API on port 8080 of the same host: untick Check the Local API for a host that only runs an agent.

Optional: create a bouncer key and paste it as Bouncer API key below.
sudo cscli bouncers add dumbmonit
In DumbMonit, enter the CrowdSec host, for example "crowdsec.lan".

steps: In the address, write the name to resolve, without "http://": "www.example.com".
Pick another record type in the options if you do not want an IPv4 address (A record).
To monitor your own DNS server, enter its IP address in "DNS server to query".
To detect hijacking, list the addresses the answer must contain in "Expected values".

ports.purpose: DNS query (default port)
DNS query too large for UDP (default port)

options.label: Record type
options.help: A for an IPv4 address, AAAA for IPv6, MX for mail, CNAME for an alias…

options.label: DNS server to query
options.help: IP address of a resolver, port optional. Empty: the system resolver. Handy to check your own DNS server.

options.label: Expected values
options.help: Values that must all appear in the answer, separated by commas. Empty: only the resolution is checked.

options.label: Comparison
options.help: "contains": each expected value must appear somewhere in the answer. "exact": the answer must hold those values and nothing else, so a record added beside the right one fails the check.

options.label: Forbidden values
options.help: Values that must never appear in the answer, separated by commas: a former host's address, an expired validation record. Checked before the expected ones.

options.label: Alert when the answer changes
options.help: Records a fingerprint of the sorted answer and alerts whenever it changes, without having to write the expected values. Leave off for names whose answer rotates between servers (large round-robin pools, geographic DNS).

options.label: Timeout (seconds)
options.help: Time after which the service is reported down if it has not answered. Between 1 and 60.

setup.title: Create a read-only service account for DumbMonit
steps:
Create the service account.
kubectl create serviceaccount dumbmonit -n kube-system

Create a ClusterRole that can only get and list what DumbMonit reads.
kubectl create clusterrole dumbmonit-read --verb=get,list --resource=nodes,pods,persistentvolumeclaims,events,deployments.apps,statefulsets.apps,daemonsets.apps

Bind the role to the service account.
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dumbmonit-read --clusterrole=dumbmonit-read --serviceaccount=kube-system:dumbmonit

Create a token that does not expire, then print the token and the cluster CA in base64.
echo '{"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Secret","metadata":{"name":"dumbmonit-token","namespace":"kube-system","annotations":{"kubernetes.io/service-account.name":"dumbmonit"}},"type":"kubernetes.io/service-account-token"}' | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n kube-system get secret dumbmonit-token -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n kube-system get secret dumbmonit-token -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}'
In DumbMonit, enter the API server address (for example https://k3s.lan:6443), paste the token as Service account token and the CA as Cluster CA certificate.

setup.title: Create a read-only user and token in Proxmox Backup Server
steps:
Open Configuration → Access Control → User Management → Add, enter the user name dumbmonit, choose the realm Proxmox Backup authentication server, then click Add.
dumbmonit@pbs

Open Configuration → Access Control → API Token → Add: user dumbmonit@pbs, token name monitor. Copy the Token ID and the Secret now, the secret is shown only once.

Open Configuration → Access Control → Permissions → Add → User Permission: path /, user dumbmonit@pbs, role Audit.

options.help: Reads the tape tier: backup jobs and their last run, drives, changers, media pools and the tapes themselves. Off by default, since most installations have no tape hardware. Needs Tape.Audit on "/tape".

options.label: Device staleness (days)
options.help: A device (phone, tablet, desktop…) with no connection and no backup for longer than this is reported stale. From 1 to 90.

label: Proxmox Datacenter Manager
summary: The console over several clusters: which instances it reaches, their failed tasks, its health.

credentials.label: API token (recommended)
credentials.help: No expiry and no session opened: the right choice for monitoring.

fields.label: Token ID
fields.help: User, realm and token name, exactly as shown when the token was created.

fields.label: Secret
fields.help: The UUID shown once when the token was created. Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Create a read-only user and token in Proxmox Datacenter Manager
steps:
Open Configuration → Access Control → Users → Add, enter the user name dumbmonit with the realm pdm and no password, then click Add.
dumbmonit@pdm

Open Configuration → Access Control → API Tokens → Add, pick that user and name the token monitor. Copy the Secret now, it is shown only once.
dumbmonit@pdm!monitor
Open Configuration → Access Control → Permissions → Add → User Permission: path /, user dumbmonit@pdm, role Auditor.
Add a second permission with Add → API Token Permission: path /, token dumbmonit@pdm!monitor, role Auditor. A token has its own permissions, so both are needed.
In DumbMonit, enter the console address (for example dc.lan:8443), the Token ID and the Secret.

ports.purpose: API (HTTPS, default)

permissions:
Auditor on /
Read-only: instances, tasks, console health

Resource.Modify on /resource (optional)
Only for the update summary of the instances
setup.warning: The console uses a self-signed certificate by default: tick "Accept an unverifiable certificate" in the options if the connection is refused.

options.label: API port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Proxmox Datacenter Manager ships with a self-signed certificate by default: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each API call, from 1 to 120. The console relays calls to every federated instance, so one slow site holds the whole answer.

options.label: Console node name
options.help: Name of the node that runs the console. A Datacenter Manager has a single node and calls it "localhost".

options.label: Task window (hours)
options.help: Older tasks are not counted among the failures, from 1 to 8760.

options.label: Accepted cache age (seconds)
options.help: How stale the console's own inventory may be before it queries the federated instances again, from 0 to 3600. Zero asks for fresh data on every probe, which puts every cluster back on the line.

options.label: Monitored instances
options.help: Names of the federated instances to monitor, separated by commas. Empty: every instance.

options.label: Instance version limit
options.help: Maximum number of instances asked for their version on each probe, from 1 to 1000.

options.label: Read each instance version
options.help: One call per federated instance, to report its version and to flag the ones left behind their peers. An instance that does not answer counts as unreachable.

options.label: Watch tasks across instances
options.help: Reads the task list of every federated instance to report the failures. Needs Resource.Audit; silently skipped otherwise.

options.label: Watch the console host
options.help: Reads the CPU, memory, root filesystem, uptime, certificates and subscription of the machine running the console. Needs Sys.Audit on "/system"; silently skipped otherwise.

options.label: Count pending updates
options.help: Lists the packages waiting for an update on the console itself. Needs Sys.Audit; silently skipped otherwise.

options.label: Count updates on each instance
options.help: Reads the console's update summary for the federated instances. Off by default: the console guards that path with Resource.Modify, a write privilege a monitoring account has no reason to hold.

label: pfSense
summary: A pfSense firewall through its REST API package: gateways down or losing packets, interfaces without link, stopped services, CPU, memory and disk.

credentials.label: REST API key
credentials.help: The key created for the dumbmonit user: it carries only that user's read privileges.

fields.label: API key
fields.help: Printed once by the key creation of step 3. Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Create a read-only REST API key for DumbMonit
steps:
Install the pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI package (version 2) from Diagnostics → Command Prompt, with the file matching your pfSense version (2.7.2 below).
pkg-static add https://github.com/pfrest/pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI/releases/latest/download/pfSense-2.7.2-pkg-RESTAPI.pkg
System → REST API → Settings: tick both BasicAuth and Key among the authentication methods.
System → User Manager → Users → Add: create the user dumbmonit with a long random password.
Edit the user and, under Assigned Privileges, add the privileges listed below.

Create the key as dumbmonit, copy the key value of the answer, then remove the POST privilege again.
curl -k -u dumbmonit -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"descr":"DumbMonit"}' https://pfsense.lan/api/v2/auth/key
In DumbMonit, enter the pfSense address (pfsense.lan) and paste the key as API key.

ports.purpose: API (HTTPS, default)
Only with the HTTP protocol option

permissions:
/api/v2/status/system GET
CPU, memory, disk, temperature

/api/v2/status/gateways GET
Gateway state, delay and loss

/api/v2/status/interfaces GET
Interface link and counters

/api/v2/status/services GET
Stopped services

/api/v2/system/version GET
pfSense version

/api/v2/system/restapi/version GET
Optional: updates of the REST API package

/api/v2/auth/key POST
Only while creating the key, then remove it

label: Pi-hole
summary: The DNS ad blocker: blocking on or paused, queries and share blocked, blocklist age, upstream failures, updates and its own diagnosis messages.
examples: Pi-hole v6 on a Raspberry Pi

credentials.label: App password (recommended)
credentials.help: Generated under Settings → Web interface / API in expert mode. It cannot change Pi-hole's settings.

fields.label: App password
fields.help: Pi-hole shows it once. Stored encrypted, never shown again.

credentials.label: No password
credentials.help: Only for a Pi-hole whose web interface has no password at all.

setup.title: Create an app password in Pi-hole
steps: In Pi-hole's web interface, open Settings → Web interface / API and switch the page from Basic to Expert.
Click Configure app password, copy the password shown, then click Enable new app password.
Check that Settings → All settings → Webserver and API → webserver.api.app_sudo is off, its default.
In DumbMonit, enter Pi-hole's address and paste the app password, or pick No password if the web interface has none.

ports.purpose: API (HTTP, default)
Only with the https scheme option

setup.warning: Pi-hole v6 or later is required; the app password can still pause blocking and edit lists through the API, so keep it for DumbMonit only.

options.label: Protocol
options.help: Pi-hole serves plain HTTP on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443 with a certificate it signs itself.

options.label: Port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Pi-hole's own HTTPS certificate is self-signed: enable this to use HTTPS without installing your own certificate.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each call, from 1 to 60.

label: Reachable host (ping)
summary: A host answers ICMP: response time and packet loss.

credentials.label: No authentication
credentials.help: Nothing is sent: the monitor answers without credentials.

setup.title: Monitor a host with ping
steps: In the address, write the host name or IP address: "192.168.1.1" or "router.home.lan".
Lower "Tolerated loss" in the options to be warned before the loss is total.
setup.warning: In Docker, keep the sysctls lines of the shipped docker-compose.yml, or the check cannot send pings.

options.label: Number of echoes
options.help: Packets sent on each poll, from 1 to 20.

options.label: Wait per packet (ms)
options.help: Time allowed for each reply, from 50 to 10,000 ms.

options.label: Gap between two echoes (ms)
options.help: Pause between two echoes, from 0 to 5,000 ms.

options.label: Payload size (bytes)
options.help: Data carried by each echo, from 0 to 1,400 bytes.

options.label: IP version
options.help: "auto" takes the first resolved address; force 4 or 6 if the host has both and one does not answer.

options.label: Tolerated loss (%)
options.help: Above this percentage of lost packets, the host is reported down. 100: only a total loss counts, partial loss stays visible in the charts.

options.label: Timeout (seconds)
options.help: Total budget for the poll, from 1 to 60. Refused if it does not cover "number of echoes × wait per packet".

label: Plex Media Server
summary: Active streams and transcodes, bandwidth, library scans, updates, read from the server itself.

credentials.label: X-Plex-Token
credentials.help: Needed by a server linked to a Plex account, unless this network is allowed without authentication.

fields.label: Token
fields.help: Stored encrypted, never shown again.

credentials.label: No token (allowed network)
credentials.help: For a server that lists DumbMonit's address among the networks allowed without authentication.

setup.title: Give DumbMonit access to the Plex server
steps: In Plex Web, open Settings → Network and click Show Advanced.

Add the DumbMonit address to List of IP addresses and networks that are allowed without auth, then save.
10.0.0.20/32
In DumbMonit, enter the server's address and pick No token.
If DumbMonit is not on your network, use the owner's token instead: open a movie → ⋯ → Get Info → View XML and copy X-Plex-Token from the page address.

ports.purpose: API (HTTP, default)

setup.warning: The token is your Plex account's and can manage the server and every library: prefer the allowed network when DumbMonit is on your own network.

options.label: Protocol
options.help: Used when the address does not start with http:// or https://.

options.label: Port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port. Choosing the other protocol without a port uses 80 or 443.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: For a self-signed or private certificate: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each call, from 1 to 120. Photo and file counts are computed on every call on a large instance.

label: Proxmox Mail Gateway
summary: Mail queues and stuck mail, spam and virus traffic, quarantine, signature age.

credentials.label: Username / password (recommended)
credentials.help: Opens a two-hour session, renewed automatically. Proxmox Mail Gateway does not issue API tokens: this is its normal way in.

fields.label: User name
fields.help: User and realm, as in "dumbmonit@pmg".

credentials.label: API token
credentials.help: Only if your gateway offers API tokens: Proxmox Mail Gateway 9 and earlier do not create any. Use the username and password instead.

fields.label: Token ID
fields.help: User, realm and token name, exactly as shown when the token was created.

fields.label: Secret
fields.help: The UUID shown once when the token was created. Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Create a read-only user in Proxmox Mail Gateway
steps:
Open Configuration → User Management → Users → Add, enter the user name below, a long password used nowhere else, and tick Enabled.
dumbmonit@pmg
Set its Role to Audit, then click Add.
In DumbMonit, enter the gateway address (for example mail.lan:8006), then this user name, realm included, and its password.

ports.purpose: API (HTTPS, default)

permissions:
Audit role
Read-only: status, queues, statistics, quarantine counts
setup.warning: Proxmox Mail Gateway has no API tokens, so DumbMonit signs in with this password. It uses a self-signed certificate by default: tick "Accept an unverifiable certificate" in the options if the connection is refused.

options.label: API port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Proxmox Mail Gateway ships with a self-signed certificate by default: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each API call, from 1 to 120. Reading a queue runs a Postfix command on the gateway and can take a few seconds.

options.label: Monitored node
options.help: Name of the cluster node to monitor. Empty: every node the gateway lists.

options.label: Traffic window (hours)
options.help: How far back the traffic curve goes, from 1 to 24. The daily totals always cover the current day.

options.label: Watch the mail queues
options.help: Reads the incoming, active, deferred and hold queues and the age of the oldest message in each. A growing deferred queue is the first sign that mail is stuck.

options.label: Count the quarantines
options.help: Reads how many messages the spam and virus quarantines hold, and how much disk they use. Counts only: no subject, sender or message content is ever read.

options.label: Also count the attachment quarantine
options.help: That quarantine has no count call: it has to be listed to be counted. Off by default; only the number of entries is kept.

options.label: Watch the signature databases
options.help: Reads the age of the ClamAV virus databases and of the SpamAssassin rule channels. Out-of-date signatures fail silently: the gateway keeps filtering, badly.

options.label: Watch the services
options.help: Reads the state of postfix, pmg-smtp-filter, pmgpolicy and the other units of each node.

options.label: Watch the certificates
options.help: Reads the certificates the web interface serves and warns before they expire.

options.label: Count pending updates
options.help: Lists the packages waiting for an update on each node. Needs the Audit role; silently skipped otherwise.

options.label: Read the subscription
options.help: Reads the subscription status of each node. An installation without a key reports "notfound", which is not an error.

label: PostgreSQL database
summary: Logs in and runs a query: catches a database that is up but no longer answering.
examples: The database behind Nextcloud or Immich

credentials.label: Username / password
credentials.help: A read-only account created for monitoring, never an application one.

fields.label: Password
fields.help: Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Monitor a PostgreSQL database
steps:
In psql, create a role that may only log in.
CREATE ROLE dumbmonit LOGIN PASSWORD 'a-long-password';

Allow it to connect from the DumbMonit host with this line in pg_hba.conf (adjust the address), then reload PostgreSQL.
host all dumbmonit 10.0.0.5/32 scram-sha-256
In DumbMonit, enter the server, for example db.home.lan:5433 (port 5432 by default), then the role's user and password.
Optional: replace the default query SELECT 1 with one that returns a single number, to chart it.

ports.purpose: PostgreSQL (default port)

permissions:
LOGIN (role attribute)
Connect only, no other privilege
setup.warning: The check opens a real connection on every poll: on an instance close to its connection limit, give it a longer interval.

options.label: Port
options.help: Used if the address does not give one.

options.label: Database
options.help: Database opened on connection. The monitoring account must be allowed to connect to it.

options.label: Query
options.help: Run on every check. The default reads no table, so the account needs no privilege beyond connecting. A query returning one number turns it into a chart.
options.placeholder: SELECT count(*) FROM jobs WHERE failed

options.label: Expected value
options.help: Value the first column of the first row must hold. Empty: only the query succeeding is checked.

options.label: Encryption
options.help: "prefer" encrypts when the server offers it, "require" refuses to connect without it, "verify-full" also checks the certificate and the name, "disable" never encrypts.

options.label: Allow loopback and link-local targets
options.help: By default the check refuses addresses only the DumbMonit host itself can reach (127.0.0.1, ::1, 169.254.x.x). Enable this to monitor a service running on the DumbMonit host. Private LAN addresses (10.x, 192.168.x) are always allowed.

options.label: Timeout (seconds)
options.help: Time after which the service is reported down if it has not answered. Between 1 and 60.

label: Proxmox VE
summary: Nodes, virtual machines, containers, storage and backups of a Proxmox server or cluster.

credentials.label: API token (recommended)
credentials.help: No expiry and no session opened: the right choice for monitoring.

fields.label: Token ID
fields.help: User, realm and token name, exactly as shown when the token was created.

fields.label: Secret
fields.help: The UUID shown once when the token was created. Stored encrypted, never shown again.

credentials.label: Username / password
credentials.help: Opens a two-hour session, renewed automatically. Use it only if tokens are not an option.

fields.label: User name
fields.help: User and realm, as in "dumbmonit@pve".

setup.title: Create a read-only user and token in Proxmox VE
steps:
Open Datacenter → Permissions → Users → Add, enter the user name dumbmonit, choose the realm Proxmox VE authentication server, then click Add.
dumbmonit@pve
Open Datacenter → Permissions → Add → User Permission: path /, user dumbmonit@pve, role PVEAuditor, then click Add.

Open Datacenter → Permissions → API Tokens → Add: user dumbmonit@pve, Token ID monitor, untick Privilege Separation, then click Add.
dumbmonit@pve!monitor
Copy the Token ID and the Secret into DumbMonit's Token ID and Secret fields. The secret is shown only once.
Optional, for the pending-updates count: Datacenter → Permissions → Roles → Create a role with only Sys.Modify, then add it as a User Permission on path /nodes.
In DumbMonit, enter the address of any node (port 8006 by default).

ports.purpose: API (HTTPS, default)

permissions:
PVEAuditor on /
Read-only: nodes, storage, VMs, containers, backups, guest agent

Sys.Modify on /nodes (optional)
Only to list pending updates

VM.Monitor on / (optional, Proxmox VE 8)
Only for the QEMU guest agent options
setup.warning: Proxmox VE uses a self-signed certificate by default: tick "Accept an unverifiable certificate" in the options if the connection is refused. On Proxmox VE 8, guest agent details also need VM.Monitor (see the guide).

options.label: API port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Proxmox ships with a self-signed certificate by default: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each API call, from 1 to 120.

options.label: Backup lookback (days)
options.help: Older backup tasks are not examined, from 1 to 3650.

options.label: Inventory backup archives
options.help: Scans the backup storages to date the last backup of each machine. Disable if the storage is slow to answer.

options.label: Monitored nodes
options.help: Names of the nodes to monitor, separated by commas. Empty: every node in the cluster.

options.label: Watch high availability
options.help: Reads the HA manager state: quorum, master, LRMs and the state of each HA resource.

options.label: Watch backup jobs
options.help: Reads the scheduled backup jobs (next run, last result) and lists the guests no job covers.

options.label: Inventory snapshots
options.help: Lists the snapshots of every VM and container to report their number and age. One API call per guest.

options.label: Snapshot inventory limit
options.help: Maximum number of guests whose snapshots are listed per probe, from 1 to 10000. Beyond it, the remaining guests are counted as skipped.

options.label: Watch replication jobs
options.help: Reads the state of ZFS replication jobs on every node.

options.label: Watch Ceph
options.help: Reads the Ceph cluster health, OSDs and usage. Silently skipped when Ceph is not set up.

options.label: Count pending updates
options.help: Lists the packages waiting for an update on each node. Needs Sys.Modify on "/nodes" (see the docs); silently skipped otherwise.

options.label: Watch node certificates
options.help: Reports the days left before each node certificate expires.

options.label: Ask the QEMU guest agent
options.help: For each running VM: balloon memory and, when the guest agent is enabled, the disk usage seen from inside (needs VM.GuestAgent.Audit, or VM.Monitor before Proxmox VE 9). Silently skipped when the agent is absent.

options.label: Watch physical disks
options.help: SMART health, wearout and temperature of every disk of each node.

options.label: Watch ZFS pools
options.help: Health, capacity and fragmentation of the ZFS pools of each node.

options.label: Detect package changes
options.help: Compares the installed Proxmox packages with the previous probe and reports an upgrade for one hour.

options.label: Watch subscription and repositories
options.help: Subscription status and APT repositories of each node (enterprise without subscription, unreadable sources).

options.label: Read the cluster inventory
options.help: One call lists every node, guest, storage and pool of the cluster. Keep it on: it is the only source that still sees the guests of a node that stopped answering, and it saves two calls per node.

options.label: Watch node services
options.help: State of the Proxmox daemons of each node (pvestatd, pveproxy, pve-cluster, corosync…) and the version installed on it. A stopped pvestatd leaves the whole cluster showing frozen numbers.

options.label: Watch node networking
options.help: Bridges, bonds and VLANs of each node with their link state, plus the traffic counters of each guest network card.

options.label: Watch LVM and thin pools
options.help: Volume groups, LVM thin pools (data and metadata fill) and PVE-managed directory mounts. A full thin pool puts every guest on it read-only.

options.label: Watch Ceph in detail
options.help: Per-OSD state, usage and latency, per-pool usage, CephFS, OSD flags and muted health checks. Needs "Watch Ceph" to be on; silently skipped when Ceph is not set up.

options.label: Check what backup jobs include
options.help: For each scheduled job, which guests it covers and which of their disks it actually writes. Catches a job that succeeds every night while skipping a data disk.

options.label: Read guest OS and addresses
options.help: Operating system and IP addresses seen from inside each running guest (QEMU guest agent for VMs, the container namespace for containers). Refreshed once an hour, not at every probe.

options.label: Ingest the full RRD metric stream
options.help: Reads /cluster/metrics/export, the stream Proxmox's own metric servers consume: everything pvestatd measures, including per-node pressure stall (PSI), and every point since the last probe rather than just the current one. Off by default: the series it adds (…_rrd_…) partly repeat the ones already collected. Needs Sys.Audit on "/".

label: Heartbeat (push)
summary: Your cron job or backup script calls DumbMonit; when it goes quiet, you are told.

credentials.label: No authentication
credentials.help: Nothing is sent: the monitor answers without credentials.

setup.title: Make the job call in
steps: In the address, write a short label for the job, unique among your heartbeats: "nightly-backup".
Set the expected interval to the job's schedule ("24h" for a nightly job), then save the monitor.

Copy the URL shown on the monitor page and call it at the end of the job.
curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 https://monit.example.com/api/push/<token>
To report a failure at once, append ?status=down&msg=... to the URL.

ports.purpose: Heartbeat call (default port, 443 behind a proxy)

setup.warning: Call the URL at the end of the job, after the part that matters: a call at the top would report a success even when the job fails.

options.label: Expected interval
options.help: How often the job is supposed to call in: 30m, 1h, 6h, 24h, 7d (or a number of seconds). A missed call is declared once this interval plus the grace period has passed.

options.label: Grace period
options.help: Extra time tolerated after the expected interval before the heartbeat counts as missed: a percentage of the interval (10%) or a fixed duration (15m). Never less than one minute.

label: RabbitMQ
summary: The message broker: memory and disk alarms that block publishers, stopped nodes and partitions, queues filling up with no consumer.

credentials.label: Username / password
credentials.help: A user tagged monitoring, sent as HTTP basic authentication.

fields.label: Password
fields.help: Stored encrypted, never shown again.

setup.title: Create a RabbitMQ monitoring user
steps: Open the RabbitMQ management interface, for example http://rabbit.lan:15672, and log in with a user allowed to manage users.
Go to Admin → Users → Add a user, name it dumbmonit, set a password and the tag monitoring, then click Add user.
Click dumbmonit in the list, and under Set permission pick each virtual host, set Configure, Write and Read to ^$, then click Set permission.
In DumbMonit, enter the address of one node, for example rabbit.lan, or https://rabbit.lan:15671 when the API is served over TLS.

ports.purpose: Management API (HTTP, default)
Only if the API is served over TLS (HTTPS, default)

permissions:
monitoring (user tag)
Read nodes, alarms and queues

Configure, Write, Read = ^$ on each virtual host
Lets it list that host's queues
setup.warning: A memory or disk alarm blocks every publisher in the cluster, and clients get no error.

options.label: Protocol
options.help: The management API listens over plain HTTP unless you configured TLS for it (usually on port 15671).

options.label: Port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: For a reverse proxy with a self-signed or private certificate: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each call, from 1 to 120.

options.label: Queues watched one by one
options.help: The fullest queues are charted one by one, up to this number (0 to 500). Totals always cover every queue.

label: Server hardware (Redfish)
summary: Fans, temperatures, power supplies, drives and memory, read from the BMC (iDRAC, iLO…).

fields.label: User name
fields.help: The read-only account created on the controller for monitoring.

setup.title: Create a read-only account on the management controller
steps: Open the web interface of the management controller (BMC), not the operating system of the server.

Create a local user named as follows, with a long password used nowhere else.
dumbmonit
Give it the read-only right of your vendor, listed below.
In DumbMonit, enter the controller address (bmc.lan or 10.0.0.50) with that user name and password.

ports.purpose: Redfish API (HTTPS, default)

permissions:
Supermicro: privilege User, account type Redfish
Configuration → Users → Add User

Dell iDRAC: role Read Only
iDRAC Settings → Users → Local Users → Add

HPE iLO: Login privilege only
Administration → User Administration → New; untick the others

Lenovo XClarity Controller: role Read-only
BMC Configuration → User/LDAP → Create

ASRock Rack: privilege User
Settings → User Management
setup.warning: Do not reuse the controller's factory account, which can power the server off and reflash the firmware; a self-signed certificate needs "Accept an unverifiable certificate" ticked.

options.label: HTTPS port
options.help: Used if the address does not give a port.

options.label: Accept an unverifiable certificate
options.help: Management controllers ship with a self-signed certificate: enable this if the connection is refused for that reason.

options.label: Timeout per request (seconds)
options.help: Time allowed for each Redfish call, from 1 to 120. A management controller is a small processor: a few seconds per answer is normal.

options.label: Authentication
options.help: basic sends the user name and password with every request and leaves nothing open on the controller. session logs in once and reuses the session token; use it only if the controller refuses basic authentication, since controllers have few session slots.

options.label: Watch the drives
options.help: Reads the storage controllers and every drive behind them: health, predicted failure, remaining SSD life. One request per drive.

options.label: Count log entries

setup.title: Create a read-only user in vSphere
steps:
On a vCenter, open Administration → Single Sign On → Users and Groups → Users, choose the domain vsphere.local, click Add and enter this user name with a long random password.

setup.title: Give DumbMonit a read-only XAPI account
steps:
On every host of the pool, create a local account with a long random password.
useradd -M -s /sbin/nologin dumbmonit
passwd dumbmonit

On the pool coordinator, turn on PAM authentication once.
xe pool-enable-external-auth auth-type=PAM service-name=pam

Register the account as a subject and note the UUID it prints.
xe subject-add subject-name=dumbmonit

Give that subject the built-in read-only role, with the UUID.
xe subject-role-add uuid=SUBJECT_UUID role-name=read-only
In DumbMonit, enter the address of the pool coordinator (for example xcp01.lan) with that user name and password.
